318: Stories, songs and laws passed on by memory
320: Before most of the Bible was written, much of its material was carried by memory: family stories, songs, genealogies, laws and sayings, retold at festivals, in homes and at shrines.
321:
The Bible itself shows a world where speech and memory carried tradition. Parents are told to teach the commandments to their children and talk about them at home and on the road. Songs like the Song of Moses and the Song of Deborah have very old poetic forms, and many scholars think they circulated orally before being written down.

The Bible also mentions writing very early: Moses is told to write a record, and Joshua writes words in a book of the law. So the picture is not 'oral first, writing later' in a neat line, but oral and written tradition existing side by side for centuries.

How long and how exactly this material was passed on is debated. Traditional Jewish and Christian views hold that Moses wrote the Torah substantially himself; many critical scholars see a longer process of oral and written sources gathered over centuries. The dates here are only a broad frame.
322: The Gezer calendar: early Hebrew-region writing
324: A small limestone tablet listing the farming seasons, dated to the 10th century BC, shows that alphabetic writing was in use in the land around the time of the early Israelite kings.
325:
The tablet was found in 1908 by the archaeologist R. A. S. Macalister. It lists months by farm work: harvesting, sowing, cutting flax, harvesting barley and so on. It may be a schoolboy's writing exercise or a memory rhyme.

Scholars debate whether its language is early Hebrew or a closely related Canaanite dialect, and whether the script should be called Phoenician or Paleo-Hebrew. Either way, it shows simple alphabetic writing was practised in the region in roughly the era the Bible assigns to David and Solomon. It does not quote any biblical text.
326: Prophets' words begin to be written down
328: Prophets such as Amos, Hosea, Isaiah and Micah spoke in the 8th century BC, and their words began to be gathered in writing, sometimes on the prophet's own instruction.
329:
Isaiah is told to write on a large tablet and to 'bind up the testimony' among his disciples, showing a circle of followers keeping his words. A century later Jeremiah dictates his prophecies to the scribe Baruch; when King Jehoiakim burns the scroll, Jeremiah dictates it again with additions. That story is one of the clearest pictures in the Bible of how a book could be written, lost, rewritten and expanded.

Scholars agree that prophetic books were collected and edited over time; they differ on how much later material was added (for example in the debate over the later chapters of Isaiah).
332: The book of Proverbs says officials of King Hezekiah copied out a further collection of Solomon's proverbs, a rare biblical note about editors at work.
333: Proverbs is openly a collection of collections: sayings of Solomon, 'words of the wise', the words of Agur, the words of King Lemuel. The heading in Proverbs 25 says Hezekiah's men 'copied' or 'transcribed' the following proverbs. Many historians think Hezekiah's reign (late 8th century BC) was a period of increased writing and literacy in Judah, partly on the evidence of inscriptions such as the Siloam tunnel inscription.
334: Josiah's 'book of the law' found in the temple
336: During temple repairs under King Josiah, the high priest Hilkiah found 'the book of the law'. Its reading led to sweeping religious reform.
337:
Kings and Chronicles tell how the scroll was read to Josiah, who tore his clothes in grief, consulted the prophetess Huldah, read the book to the people, renewed the covenant and kept a great Passover.

What was the book? Since the early church (Jerome and others) many have linked it with Deuteronomy, because Josiah's reforms (one central place of worship, removal of idols, Passover in Jerusalem) match Deuteronomy's commands closely. Traditional readers see it as a lost copy of the Mosaic law rediscovered; many critical scholars think Deuteronomy, at least in its core, was composed or edited not long before and 'found' as a reform document. Both groups agree the event shows a written book carrying authority over king and people.
338: Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls carry the priestly blessing
340: Two tiny rolled silver amulets from a burial cave in Jerusalem contain a form of the priestly blessing from Numbers 6, the oldest known text closely matching a biblical passage.
341:
Gabriel Barkay's team found the amulets in 1979. Unrolling and reading them took years; a high-resolution re-study published in 2004 confirmed a late 7th or early 6th century BC date, around the time of Jeremiah and just before the Babylonian exile.

The text is close to 'The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face shine upon you... and give you peace', though shorter than the full Numbers form. They were worn as protective charms, which also tells us how ordinary people used sacred words. They do not prove when the book of Numbers as a whole was finished, but they show this blessing was already known and written before the exile.
342: Exile: preserving Israel's writings in Babylon
344: After Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, exiled scribes and priests in Babylon kept and edited Israel's histories, laws, psalms and prophecies.
345:
Many scholars think the exile was a key period for gathering Israel's traditions, since the temple was gone and the written word became the centre of identity. Ezekiel prophesied among the exiles, Daniel is said to have read Jeremiah's scroll, and Psalm 137 voices exile grief.

How much was written versus edited in this time is debated. Traditional views stress preservation of older texts; critical views often place major editing (for example of the books from Joshua to Kings) in or around this period.
346: Ezra reads the law to the people
348: Ezra the scribe read the book of the law of Moses aloud from morning to midday while Levites helped the people understand it, a founding scene for public Bible reading and teaching.
349:
Ezra is described as a scribe skilled in the law of Moses who set his heart to study, do and teach it. In Nehemiah 8 the law is read from a wooden platform, the people stand, and Levites 'give the sense' so the people understand, which some see as an early form of translation or explanation into Aramaic.

Jewish tradition later credited Ezra and the 'men of the Great Assembly' with major roles in arranging the scriptures, and some ancient writers even said Ezra restored lost books (a legend in the non-canonical book 2 Esdras 14). Historians treat these later stories with caution, but agree that by Ezra's time the Torah functioned as written, public authority. The exact date (458 or 445 BC, or later) depends on how one dates Ezra relative to Nehemiah.
350: The Septuagint: the Hebrew Scriptures in Greek
352: Greek-speaking Jews in Alexandria translated the Torah into Greek in the 3rd century BC; the rest of the books followed over the next two centuries. This 'Septuagint' became the Bible of most early Christians.
353:
The name means 'seventy' (shortened LXX) from a legend in the *Letter of Aristeas*: King Ptolemy II asked for the Jewish law for his library, and 72 elders from Jerusalem translated it in 72 days with perfect agreement. Later writers (Philo, then Christian authors) embellished this into separate cells producing identical translations.

Historians treat the letter as a legend written to give the translation authority. What is solid: the Torah was translated in Alexandria around the mid-3rd century BC, probably mainly for Greek-speaking Jews who no longer read Hebrew well; other books were translated by different people, in different styles, over a long period.

The Septuagint matters because the New Testament writers often quote it, because it sometimes reflects a Hebrew text different from the later standard (as the Dead Sea Scrolls confirmed), and because it includes extra books (the deuterocanon or Apocrypha) that shaped the later canon debates.
356: Between about 250 BC and AD 68, scribes copied the scrolls later hidden in caves near Qumran, including more than 200 manuscripts of biblical books.
357:
The Qumran collection holds roughly 900 or more manuscripts in fragments. About a quarter are copies of books in the Hebrew Bible; every book except Esther is represented at least by fragments. There are also commentaries, rules for a community, hymns and other writings.

The scrolls show that in the late Second Temple period several forms of the Hebrew text circulated side by side: some very close to the later Masoretic text, some closer to the Hebrew behind the Septuagint, some resembling the Samaritan Pentateuch. Who owned them (often linked to the Essenes) is debated, but the copying dates are widely accepted from handwriting study and radiocarbon tests. The community settlement was destroyed by the Romans around AD 68.
358: Jesus reads from an Isaiah scroll in Nazareth
360: Luke describes Jesus being handed the scroll of Isaiah in the synagogue, unrolling it and reading, a glimpse of how scripture was used in his day.
361: The scene shows scrolls kept in a village synagogue, read publicly on the Sabbath and explained. Elsewhere Jesus refers to 'the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms', a phrase many see as an early way of naming the three parts of the Hebrew scriptures, and to the blood of the prophets 'from Abel to Zechariah', which some read as spanning the Hebrew Bible from Genesis to Chronicles (its last book in Jewish order). That second reading is suggestive but debated.
362: The New Testament books are written
364: Paul's letters (from about AD 48-50 to the 60s), the Gospels (roughly AD 65-95 on most views), and the other letters and Revelation were written within about two generations of Jesus.
365:
1 Thessalonians or Galatians is usually counted the earliest surviving Christian writing (around AD 49-51). Most scholars date Mark around 65-70, Matthew and Luke around 80-90, John around 90-100, and Revelation in the mid-90s, though conservative scholars often place the Synoptic Gospels and Acts before AD 70, partly because Acts ends with Paul still alive in Rome.

The authorship of some letters (for example the Pastoral letters, 2 Peter, Ephesians) is debated among scholars; traditional views accept the named authors. The books were written in Koine (common) Greek, as letters and accounts for real churches, not at first as 'scripture' in a bound volume.
368: Churches swapped and copied Paul's letters, and by about AD 100 collections of them were circulating; 2 Peter already speaks of 'all his letters' alongside 'the other scriptures'.
369:
Paul himself asked that letters be read in other churches. Early writers such as Clement of Rome (around 96) and Ignatius and Polycarp (around 110) know several of Paul's letters. The earliest surviving manuscript collection, Papyrus 46 from about AD 200, contains ten letters including Hebrews.

How the collection formed is debated: some think a single person (perhaps Onesimus, or a Pauline circle) gathered it; others think it grew gradually as churches exchanged copies.
372: Marcion, a wealthy shipowner, rejected the Old Testament and accepted only an edited Gospel of Luke and ten letters of Paul. The church excommunicated him around 144.
373:
Marcion taught that the God of the Old Testament was a different, lesser god from the Father revealed by Jesus. So he cut out the Jewish scriptures and edited out passages he saw as Jewish additions. His list is often called the first known Christian 'canon'.

Scholars debate how much Marcion pushed the church to define its own list. Older studies (Harnack) gave him a big role; many now think the church was already using the Gospels and Paul widely, and that Marcion sped up and sharpened the process rather than starting it. What we know of him comes from opponents such as Irenaeus and Tertullian.
375: Justin Martyr describes Christians meeting on Sunday to hear 'the memoirs of the apostles' or the writings of the prophets read aloud, as long as time allows.
376: Justin's *First Apology* (around 150-155) is one of the earliest descriptions of a Christian service. Reading the Gospels alongside the Old Testament prophets in worship was a key step toward treating them as scripture. Justin's student Tatian later combined the four Gospels into one continuous narrative, the *Diatessaron* (around 170), which was widely used in Syriac-speaking churches.
379: Bishop Irenaeus of Lyon argued that there are four Gospels, no more and no fewer, comparing them to the four winds and four corners of the earth.
380:
Writing around 180 against various groups that used fewer Gospels or extra 'secret' ones, Irenaeus insists on Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. His argument from the four winds is symbolic rather than proof, but it shows that a fourfold Gospel was already established in major churches.

Irenaeus also links the four Gospels with the four living creatures of Revelation and Ezekiel, the origin of the later artistic symbols of the Evangelists (lion, ox, man, eagle), though the matching of creature to Gospel varied among writers.
381: The Muratorian fragment lists New Testament books
383: A damaged Latin list of accepted books, found in an 8th-century manuscript, may be the oldest surviving New Testament canon list. Its date is debated: late 2nd century or 4th century.
384:
Ludovico Antonio Muratori found the list in the Ambrosian Library in Milan and published it in 1740. The copy is poor Latin and begins mid-sentence. It accepts four Gospels (Luke and John named; Matthew and Mark probably in the lost start), Acts, thirteen letters of Paul, Jude, two (perhaps three) letters of John, the Wisdom of Solomon, Revelation and the Apocalypse of Peter (noting some will not read it in church). It rejects forged letters of Paul and says the *Shepherd of Hermas* may be read but not in public worship, because it was written 'recently, in our times'.

That remark about Hermas is the main reason many date the list around 170-200. Albert Sundberg and Geoffrey Hahneman argued for a 4th-century Eastern origin; most scholars still favour the earlier date, but the question remains open.
385: First translations: Old Latin, Syriac and Coptic
387: As the church spread beyond Greek speakers, believers translated the scriptures into Latin, Syriac and Coptic, usually piecemeal and by different hands.
388: By the late 2nd century Latin versions were being read in North Africa (the martyrs of Scilli in 180 had 'books and letters of Paul'). Syriac Gospels existed both as Tatian's combined *Diatessaron* and as separate Gospels (the Old Syriac). Coptic translations in Egypt appear in the 3rd century. These versions matter for textual critics because they show what Greek text the translators had in front of them, sometimes earlier than any surviving Greek copy.
391: The scholar Origen laid out the Old Testament in six parallel columns (Hebrew, Hebrew in Greek letters, and four Greek versions) to compare the Septuagint with the Hebrew.
392:
Origen noticed that Greek copies differed among themselves and from the Hebrew text used by Jews. In his huge *Hexapla* ('sixfold') he set side by side the Hebrew, a Greek transliteration, the Greek versions of Aquila and Symmachus, his own revised Septuagint, and Theodotion. He used critical signs (the obelus for words in Greek but not in Hebrew, the asterisk for words added from the Hebrew).

The whole work was enormous, perhaps over 6,000 pages, and was probably never copied in full. It was kept at Caesarea, used by Eusebius and Jerome, and likely lost when the city fell in the 7th century. Fragments survive. It is an early example of textual criticism, and it also mixed the Septuagint text in ways later scholars must untangle.
395: The Great Persecution began with an edict ordering churches destroyed and Christian scriptures handed over and burned.
396:
Officials demanded the church's books. Some Christians handed them over to save their lives and were later called *traditores*, 'those who handed over', from which the word 'traitor' comes. Others hid books or gave up other texts instead, and some died rather than surrender them.

The persecution destroyed many copies, which is one reason so few manuscripts survive from before about 300. It also forced churches to decide which books were worth dying for, sharpening the question of the canon. Arguments over how to treat the *traditores* later caused the Donatist split in North Africa.
397: Eusebius sorts the books into accepted, disputed and rejected
398: The church historian Eusebius reported which books were universally accepted, which were 'disputed' though widely known (James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John), and which were spurious or heretical.
399: Eusebius' list is valuable because it shows the state of debate in the early 4th century. The four Gospels, Acts, Paul's letters, 1 John and 1 Peter were accepted everywhere. Revelation he placed awkwardly in both the accepted and the spurious columns, reflecting real division over it in the East. Hebrews was generally accepted in the East but doubted in the West, largely over its authorship.
400: Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus are made
402: The two oldest nearly complete Greek Bibles were produced in the 4th century, Vaticanus around 300-325 and Sinaiticus around 330-360.
403: These large parchment books, written in capital letters (uncials), contain both Testaments and some extra books. They are central witnesses for modern editions of the Greek New Testament and important for the Septuagint. Where they were made is debated: Alexandria and Caesarea are the two main proposals.
406: Emperor Constantine asked Eusebius to supply fifty finely written copies of the scriptures on parchment for the churches of his new capital.
407: Eusebius quotes the emperor's letter in his *Life of Constantine*. It marks a turn from persecution to imperial sponsorship of Bible production. Some have suggested that Codex Sinaiticus or Vaticanus might be among the fifty, but there is no proof, and the letter does not say which books were included. A popular myth says Constantine or the Council of Nicaea 'chose the books of the Bible'; there is no evidence Nicaea discussed the canon at all.
408: Eastern lists: Cyril of Jerusalem and Laodicea
410: In the mid-4th century, Eastern teachers such as Cyril of Jerusalem gave lists of the books to be read, generally leaving out Revelation.
411: Cyril's *Catechetical Lectures* (around 350) list 26 New Testament books, without Revelation, and urge new believers not to read books outside them. A list attached to the canons of the Council of Laodicea (around 363) is similar, though scholars doubt the list was part of the original council decisions. Revelation remained doubted in parts of the East for centuries, and the Syriac Peshitta did not include it.
412: Ulfilas invents an alphabet for the Gothic Bible
414: The missionary bishop Ulfilas created a Gothic alphabet and translated the Bible from Greek, reportedly leaving out the books of Kings as too warlike for the Goths.
415: The Gothic Bible is the oldest substantial literature in any Germanic language. The finest surviving copy is the 6th-century *Codex Argenteus* ('silver book'), written in silver and gold ink on purple parchment, now in Uppsala, Sweden. The report about Kings comes from the historian Philostorgius. Ulfilas was an Arian (he denied that the Son is fully equal with the Father), which affected later views of his work but not much of the translation itself.
416: Athanasius lists the 27 New Testament books
418: In his 39th Festal Letter, Bishop Athanasius listed exactly the 27 books of today's New Testament, the earliest known list to match it precisely.
419:
Each Easter the bishop of Alexandria sent a letter to the churches. In 367 Athanasius used his to name the 'springs of salvation'. His Old Testament list follows the Hebrew books (with Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah attached to Jeremiah, and without Esther), and he names other books such as Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the *Didache* and the *Shepherd* as useful to be read by new converts but not part of the canon.

The letter did not settle matters everywhere; it reflects and strengthens a consensus that was forming. Note that 'canon' here means a recognised list, not a book created by a decree.
422: Pope Damasus asked Jerome to revise the messy Old Latin Gospels; Jerome went on to translate most of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew. His work became the 'Vulgate', the Western church's Bible for a thousand years.
423:
Jerome revised the Gospels first (around 383-384), working from Greek manuscripts. Settling in Bethlehem, he learned Hebrew with Jewish teachers and translated the Hebrew books (around 390-405), a choice criticised by Augustine and others who trusted the Septuagint. Jerome called the books outside the Hebrew canon *apocrypha* and doubted their canonical status, though he translated Tobit and Judith and they stayed in Latin Bibles.

The rest of the New Testament in the Vulgate was revised more lightly, possibly by others. 'Vulgate' (common) became the standard name only later. It shaped Western theology and vocabulary: words like 'sacrament', 'justification' and 'penance' entered through Latin.
424: African councils at Hippo and Carthage list the books
425: Hippo Regius and Carthage, North Africa
426: Regional councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397, again 419) listed the books to be read in church: the 27-book New Testament and an Old Testament including books such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach and Maccabees.
427: Augustine took part and gave a similar list in *On Christian Teaching*. These councils were local, not universal, and the record of Hippo survives through a later summary. Their wider Old Testament list follows the Greek/Latin church's usage and is the ancestor of the Catholic canon later defined at Trent. Protestants later followed Jerome's preference for the Hebrew canon. Both sides appeal to the early church, which in fact shows genuine variety on the Old Testament.
430: By the early 5th century the Peshitta ('simple' version) was the standard Bible of Syriac churches, with a 22-book New Testament lacking 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation.
431: The Peshitta Old Testament was probably translated from Hebrew in the 2nd century, possibly with Jewish involvement. The New Testament form was standardised around the early 5th century, replacing Tatian's *Diatessaron* in church use; Bishop Rabbula of Edessa is often credited, though this is debated. Some Syriac-speaking churches (such as the Church of the East) still use the 22-book New Testament.
432: The Masoretes mark vowels, accents and notes
434: Jewish scholars called Masoretes added vowel signs, accent marks and detailed margin notes to the consonantal Hebrew text to fix its reading and protect it from copying errors.
